units.leftText: These are the words of the Teacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem:
units.rightText: The words of the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem.
leftNotes: 1:1 Or the Convener or the Preacher or the leader of the assembly; Hebrew Qoheleth is rendered as the Teacher throughout Ecclesiastes.

units.leftText: “Futility of futilities,” says the Teacher, “futility of futilities! Everything is futile!”
units.rightText: Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher; vanity of vanities, all is vanity.
leftNotes: 1:2 Literally vapor or breath; the Hebrew words translated in Ecclesiastes as forms of futile or fleeting can also be translated as vanity or meaningless.

units.leftText: What does a man gain from all his labor, at which he toils under the sun?
units.rightText: What profit hath man of all his labor wherein he laboreth under the sun?

units.leftText: Generations come and generations go, but the earth remains forever.
units.rightText: One generation goeth, and another generation cometh; but the earth abideth for ever.

units.leftText: The sun rises and the sun sets; it hurries back to where it rises.
units.rightText: The sun also ariseth, and the sun goeth down, and hasteth to its place where it ariseth.

units.leftText: The wind blows southward, then turns northward; round and round it swirls, ever returning on its course.
units.rightText: The wind goeth toward the south, and turneth about unto the north; it turneth about continually in its course, and the wind returneth again to its circuits.

units.leftText: All the rivers flow into the sea, yet the sea is never full; to the place from which the streams come, there again they flow.
units.rightText: All the rivers run into the sea, yet the sea is not full; unto the place whither the rivers go, thither they go again.

units.leftText: All things are wearisome, more than one can describe; the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear content with hearing.
units.rightText: All things are full of weariness; man cannot utter it: the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing.

units.leftText: What has been will be again, and what has been done will be done again; there is nothing new under the sun.
units.rightText: That which hath been is that which shall be; and that which hath been done is that which shall be done: and there is no new thing under the sun.

units.leftText: Is there a case where one can say, “Look, this is new”? It has already existed in the ages before us.
units.rightText: Is there a thing whereof it may be said, See, this is new? it hath been long ago, in the ages which were before us.

units.leftText: There is no remembrance of those who came before, and those yet to come will not be remembered by those who follow after. With Wisdom Comes Sorrow
units.rightText: There is no remembrance of the former generations; neither shall there be any remembrance of the latter generations that are to come, among those that shall come after.

units.leftText: I, the Teacher, was king over Israel in Jerusalem.
units.rightText: I the Preacher was king over Israel in Jerusalem.

units.leftText: And I set my mind to seek and explore by wisdom all that is done under heaven. What a miserable task God has laid upon the sons of men to occupy them!
units.rightText: And I applied my heart to seek and to search out by wisdom concerning all that is done under heaven: it is a sore travail that God hath given to the sons of men to be exercised therewith.

units.leftText: I have seen all the things that are done under the sun, and have found them all to be futile, a pursuit of the wind.
units.rightText: I have seen all the works that are done under the sun; and, behold, all is vanity and a striving after wind.

units.leftText: What is crooked cannot be straightened, and what is lacking cannot be counted.
units.rightText: That which is crooked cannot be made straight; and that which is wanting cannot be numbered.

units.leftText: I said to myself, “Behold, I have grown and increased in wisdom beyond all those before me who were over Jerusalem, and my mind has observed a wealth of wisdom and knowledge.”
units.rightText: I communed with mine own heart, saying, Lo, I have gotten me great wisdom above all that were before me in Jerusalem; yea, my heart hath had great experience of wisdom and knowledge.

units.leftText: So I set my mind to know wisdom and madness and folly; I learned that this, too, is a pursuit of the wind.
units.rightText: And I applied my heart to know wisdom, and to know madness and folly: I perceived that this also was a striving after wind.

units.leftText: For with much wisdom comes much sorrow, and as knowledge grows, grief increases.
units.rightText: For in much wisdom is much grief; and he that increaseth knowledge increaseth sorrow.

units.leftText: I said to myself, “Come now, I will test you with pleasure; enjoy what is good!” But it proved to be futile.
units.rightText: I said in my heart, Come now, I will prove thee with mirth; therefore enjoy pleasure: and, behold, this also was vanity.

units.leftText: I said of laughter, “It is folly,” and of pleasure, “What does it accomplish?”
units.rightText: I said of laughter, It is mad; and of mirth, What doeth it?

units.leftText: I sought to cheer my body with wine and to embrace folly— my mind still guiding me with wisdom— until I could see what was worthwhile for men to do under heaven during the few days of their lives.
units.rightText: I searched in my heart how to cheer my flesh with wine, my heart yet guiding me with wisdom, and how to lay hold on folly, till I might see what it was good for the sons of men that they should do under heaven all the days of their life.

units.leftText: I expanded my pursuits. I built houses and planted vineyards for myself.
units.rightText: I made me great works; I builded me houses; I planted me vineyards;

units.leftText: I made gardens and parks for myself, where I planted all kinds of fruit trees.
units.rightText: I made me gardens and parks, and I planted trees in them of all kinds of fruit;

units.leftText: I built reservoirs to water my groves of flourishing trees.
units.rightText: I made me pools of water, to water therefrom the forest where trees were reared;

units.leftText: I acquired menservants and maidservants, and servants were born in my house. I also owned more herds and flocks than anyone in Jerusalem before me,
units.rightText: I bought men-servants and maid-servants, and had servants born in my house; also I had great possessions of herds and flocks, above all that were before me in Jerusalem;

units.leftText: and I accumulated for myself silver and gold and the treasure of kings and provinces. I gathered to myself male and female singers, and the delights of the sons of men — many concubines.
units.rightText: I gathered me also silver and gold, and the treasure of kings and of the provinces; I gat me men-singers and women-singers, and the delights of the sons of men, musical instruments, and that of all sorts.

units.leftText: So I became great and surpassed all in Jerusalem who had preceded me; and my wisdom remained with me.
units.rightText: So I was great, and increased more than all that were before me in Jerusalem: also my wisdom remained with me.

units.leftText: Anything my eyes desired, I did not deny myself. I refused my heart no pleasure. For my heart took delight in all my work, and this was the reward for all my labor.
units.rightText: And whatsoever mine eyes desired I kept not from them; I withheld not my heart from any joy; for my heart rejoiced because of all my labor; and this was my portion from all my labor.

units.leftText: Yet when I considered all the works that my hands had accomplished and what I had toiled to achieve, I found everything to be futile, a pursuit of the wind; there was nothing to be gained under the sun. The Wise and the Foolish
units.rightText: Then I looked on all the works that my hands had wrought, and on the labor that I had labored to do; and, behold, all was vanity and a striving after wind, and there was no profit under the sun.

units.leftText: Then I turned to consider wisdom and madness and folly; for what more can the king’s successor do than what has already been accomplished?
units.rightText: And I turned myself to behold wisdom, and madness, and folly: for what can the man do that cometh after the king? even that which hath been done long ago.

units.leftText: And I saw that wisdom exceeds folly, just as light exceeds darkness:
units.rightText: Then I saw that wisdom excelleth folly, as far as light excelleth darkness.

units.leftText: The wise man has eyes in his head, but the fool walks in darkness.
units.rightText: The wise man’s eyes are in his head, and the fool walketh in darkness: and yet I perceived that one event happeneth to them all.

units.leftText: So I said to myself, “The fate of the fool will also befall me. What then have I gained by being wise?” And I said to myself that this too is futile.
units.rightText: Then said I in my heart, As it happeneth to the fool, so will it happen even to me; and why was I then more wise? Then said I in my heart, that this also is vanity.

units.leftText: For there is no lasting remembrance of the wise, just as with the fool, seeing that both will be forgotten in the days to come. Alas, the wise man will die just like the fool!
units.rightText: For of the wise man, even as of the fool, there is no remembrance for ever; seeing that in the days to come all will have been long forgotten. And how doth the wise man die even as the fool!

units.leftText: So I hated life, because the work that is done under the sun was grievous to me. For everything is futile and a pursuit of the wind. The Futility of Work
units.rightText: So I hated life, because the work that is wrought under the sun was grievous unto me; for all is vanity and a striving after wind.

units.leftText: I hated all for which I had toiled under the sun, because I must leave it to the man who comes after me.
units.rightText: And I hated all my labor wherein I labored under the sun, seeing that I must leave it unto the man that shall be after me.

units.leftText: And who knows whether that man will be wise or foolish? Yet he will take over all the labor at which I have worked skillfully under the sun. This too is futile.
units.rightText: And who knoweth whether he will be a wise man or a fool? yet will he have rule over all my labor wherein I have labored, and wherein I have showed myself wise under the sun. This also is vanity.

units.leftText: So my heart began to despair over all the labor that I had done under the sun.
units.rightText: Therefore I turned about to cause my heart to despair concerning all the labor wherein I had labored under the sun.

units.leftText: When there is a man who has labored with wisdom, knowledge, and skill, and he must give his portion to a man who has not worked for it, this too is futile and a great evil.
units.rightText: For there is a man whose labor is with wisdom, and with knowledge, and with skilfulness; yet to a man that hath not labored therein shall he leave it for his portion. This also is vanity and a great evil.

units.leftText: For what does a man get for all the toil and striving with which he labors under the sun?
units.rightText: For what hath a man of all his labor, and of the striving of his heart, wherein he laboreth under the sun?

units.leftText: Indeed, all his days are filled with grief, and his task is sorrowful; even at night, his mind does not rest. This too is futile.
units.rightText: For all his days are but sorrows, and his travail is grief; yea, even in the night his heart taketh no rest. This also is vanity.

units.leftText: Nothing is better for a man than to eat and drink and enjoy his work. I have also seen that this is from the hand of God.
units.rightText: There is nothing better for a man than that he should eat and drink, and make his soul enjoy good in his labor. This also I saw, that it is from the hand of God.

units.leftText: For apart from Him, who can eat and who can find enjoyment?
units.rightText: For who can eat, or who can have enjoyment, more than I?
leftNotes: 2:25 Some Hebrew manuscripts, LXX, Syriac; most Hebrew manuscripts apart from me or more than I

units.leftText: To the man who is pleasing in His sight, He gives wisdom and knowledge and joy, but to the sinner He assigns the task of gathering and accumulating that which he will hand over to one who pleases God. This too is futile and a pursuit of the wind.
units.rightText: For to the man that pleaseth him God giveth wisdom, and knowledge, and joy; but to the sinner he giveth travail, to gather and to heap up, that he may give to him that pleaseth God. This also is vanity and a striving after wind.

units.leftText: To everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven:
units.rightText: For everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven:

units.leftText: a time to be born and a time to die, a time to plant and a time to uproot,
units.rightText: a time to be born, and a time to die; a time to plant, and a time to pluck up that which is planted;

units.leftText: a time to kill and a time to heal, a time to break down and a time to build,
units.rightText: a time to kill, and a time to heal; a time to break down, and a time to build up;

units.leftText: a time to weep and a time to laugh, a time to mourn and a time to dance,
units.rightText: a time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;

units.leftText: a time to cast away stones and a time to gather stones together, a time to embrace and a time to refrain from embracing,
units.rightText: a time to cast away stones, and a time to gather stones together; a time to embrace, and a time to refrain from embracing;

units.leftText: a time to search and a time to count as lost, a time to keep and a time to discard,
units.rightText: a time to seek, and a time to lose; a time to keep, and a time to cast away;

units.leftText: a time to tear and a time to mend, a time to be silent and a time to speak,
units.rightText: a time to rend, and a time to sew; a time to keep silence, and a time to speak;

units.leftText: a time to love and a time to hate, a time for war and a time for peace. God’s Works Remain Forever
units.rightText: a time to love, and a time to hate; a time for war, and a time for peace.

units.leftText: What does the worker gain from his toil?
units.rightText: What profit hath he that worketh in that wherein he laboreth?

units.leftText: I have seen the burden that God has laid upon the sons of men to occupy them.
units.rightText: I have seen the travail which God hath given to the sons of men to be exercised therewith.

units.leftText: He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also set eternity in the hearts of men, yet they cannot fathom the work that God has done from beginning to end.
units.rightText: He hath made everything beautiful in its time: also he hath set eternity in their heart, yet so that man cannot find out the work that God hath done from the beginning even to the end.

units.leftText: I know that there is nothing better for them than to rejoice and do good while they live,
units.rightText: I know that there is nothing better for them, than to rejoice, and to do good so long as they live.

units.leftText: and also that every man should eat and drink and find satisfaction in all his labor — this is the gift of God.
units.rightText: And also that every man should eat and drink, and enjoy good in all his labor, is the gift of God.

units.leftText: I know that everything God does endures forever; nothing can be added to it or taken from it. God does it so that they should fear Him.
units.rightText: I know that, whatsoever God doeth, it shall be for ever: nothing can be put to it, nor anything taken from it; and God hath done it, that men should fear before him.

units.leftText: What exists has already been, and what will be has already been, for God will call to account what has passed. From Dust to Dust
units.rightText: That which is hath been long ago; and that which is to be hath long ago been: and God seeketh again that which is passed away.

units.leftText: Furthermore, I saw under the sun that in the place of judgment there is wickedness, and in the place of righteousness there is wickedness.
units.rightText: And moreover I saw under the sun, in the place of justice, that wickedness was there; and in the place of righteousness, that wickedness was there.

units.leftText: I said in my heart, “God will judge the righteous and the wicked, since there is a time for every activity and every deed.”
units.rightText: I said in my heart, God will judge the righteous and the wicked; for there is a time there for every purpose and for every work.

units.leftText: I said to myself, “As for the sons of men, God tests them so that they may see for themselves that they are but beasts.”
units.rightText: I said in my heart, It is because of the sons of men, that God may prove them, and that they may see that they themselves are but as beasts.

units.leftText: For the fates of both men and beasts are the same: As one dies, so dies the other — they all have the same breath. Man has no advantage over the animals, since everything is futile.
units.rightText: For that which befalleth the sons of men befalleth beasts; even one thing befalleth them: as the one dieth, so dieth the other; yea, they have all one breath; and man hath no preeminence above the beasts: for all is vanity.

units.leftText: All go to one place; all come from dust, and all return to dust.
units.rightText: All go unto one place; all are of the dust, and all turn to dust again.

units.leftText: Who knows if the spirit of man rises upward and the spirit of the animal descends into the earth?
units.rightText: Who knoweth the spirit of man, whether it goeth upward, and the spirit of the beast, whether it goeth downward to the earth?

units.leftText: I have seen that there is nothing better for a man than to enjoy his work, because that is his lot. For who can bring him to see what will come after him?
units.rightText: Wherefore I saw that there is nothing better, than that a man should rejoice in his works; for that is his portion: for who shall bring him back to see what shall be after him?

units.leftText: Again I looked, and I considered all the oppression taking place under the sun. I saw the tears of the oppressed, and they had no comforter; the power lay in the hands of their oppressors, and there was no comforter.
units.rightText: Then I returned and saw all the oppressions that are done under the sun: and, behold, the tears of such as were oppressed, and they had no comforter; and on the side of their oppressors there was power; but they had no comforter.

units.leftText: So I admired the dead, who had already died, above the living, who are still alive.
units.rightText: Wherefore I praised the dead that have been long dead more than the living that are yet alive;

units.leftText: But better than both is he who has not yet existed, who has not seen the evil that is done under the sun.
units.rightText: yea, better than them both did I esteem him that hath not yet been, who hath not seen the evil work that is done under the sun.

units.leftText: I saw that all labor and success spring from a man’s envy of his neighbor. This too is futile and a pursuit of the wind.
units.rightText: Then I saw all labor and every skilful work, that for this a man is envied of his neighbor. This also is vanity and a striving after wind.

units.leftText: The fool folds his hands and consumes his own flesh.
units.rightText: The fool foldeth his hands together, and eateth his own flesh.

units.leftText: Better one handful with tranquility than two handfuls with toil and pursuit of the wind.
units.rightText: Better is a handful, with quietness, than two handfuls with labor and striving after wind.

units.leftText: Again, I saw futility under the sun.
units.rightText: Then I returned and saw vanity under the sun.

units.leftText: There is a man all alone, without even a son or brother. And though there is no end to his labor, his eyes are still not content with his wealth: “For whom do I toil and bereave my soul of enjoyment?” This too is futile — a miserable task.
units.rightText: There is one that is alone, and he hath not a second; yea, he hath neither son nor brother; yet is there no end of all his labor, neither are his eyes satisfied with riches. For whom then, saith he, do I labor, and deprive my soul of good? This also is vanity, yea, it is a sore travail.

units.leftText: Two are better than one, because they have a good return for their labor.
units.rightText: Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor.

units.leftText: For if one falls down, his companion can lift him up; but pity the one who falls without another to help him up!
units.rightText: For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him that is alone when he falleth, and hath not another to lift him up.

units.leftText: Again, if two lie down together, they will keep warm; but how can one keep warm alone?
units.rightText: Again, if two lie together, then they have warmth; but how can one be warm alone?

units.leftText: And though one may be overpowered, two can resist. Moreover, a cord of three strands is not quickly broken. The Futility of Power
units.rightText: And if a man prevail against him that is alone, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.

units.leftText: Better is a poor but wise youth than an old but foolish king who no longer knows how to take a warning.
units.rightText: Better is a poor and wise youth than an old and foolish king, who knoweth not how to receive admonition any more.

units.leftText: For the youth has come from the prison to the kingship, though he was born poor in his own kingdom.
units.rightText: For out of prison he came forth to be king; yea, even in his kingdom he was born poor.

units.leftText: I saw that all who lived and walked under the sun followed this second one, the youth who succeeded the king.
units.rightText: I saw all the living that walk under the sun, that they were with the youth, the second, that stood up in his stead.

units.leftText: There is no limit to all the people who were before them. Yet the successor will not be celebrated by those who come even later. This too is futile and a pursuit of the wind.
units.rightText: There was no end of all the people, even of all them over whom he was: yet they that come after shall not rejoice in him. Surely this also is vanity and a striving after wind.

units.leftText: Guard your steps when you go to the house of God. Draw near to listen rather than to offer the sacrifice of fools, who do not know that they do wrong.
units.rightText: Keep thy foot when thou goest to the house of God; for to draw nigh to hear is better than to give the sacrifice of fools: for they know not that they do evil.

units.leftText: Do not be quick to speak, and do not be hasty in your heart to utter a word before God. For God is in heaven and you are on earth. So let your words be few.
units.rightText: Be not rash with thy mouth, and let not thy heart be hasty to utter anything before God; for God is in heaven, and thou upon earth: therefore let thy words be few.

units.leftText: As a dream comes through many cares, so the speech of a fool comes with many words.
units.rightText: For a dream cometh with a multitude of business, and a fool’s voice with a multitude of words.

units.leftText: When you make a vow to God, do not delay in fulfilling it, because He takes no pleasure in fools. Fulfill your vow.
units.rightText: When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou vowest.

units.leftText: It is better not to vow than to make a vow and not fulfill it.
units.rightText: Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay.

units.leftText: Do not let your mouth cause your flesh to sin, and do not tell the messenger that your vow was a mistake. Why should God be angry with your words and destroy the work of your hands?
units.rightText: Suffer not thy mouth to cause thy flesh to sin; neither say thou before the angel, that it was an error: wherefore should God be angry at thy voice, and destroy the work of thy hands?

units.leftText: For as many dreams bring futility, so do many words. Therefore, fear God. The Futility of Wealth (Psalm 49:1–20|PSA 49:1-20*)
units.rightText: For in the multitude of dreams there are vanities, and in many words: but fear thou God.

units.leftText: If you see the oppression of the poor and the denial of justice and righteousness in the province, do not be astonished at the matter; for one official is watched by a superior, and others higher still are over them.
units.rightText: If thou seest the oppression of the poor, and the violent taking away of justice and righteousness in a province, marvel not at the matter: for one higher than the high regardeth; and there are higher than they.

units.leftText: The produce of the earth is taken by all; the king himself profits from the fields.
units.rightText: Moreover the profit of the earth is for all: the king himself is served by the field.

units.leftText: He who loves money is never satisfied by money, and he who loves wealth is never satisfied by income. This too is futile.
units.rightText: He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver; nor he that loveth abundance, with increase: this also is vanity.

units.leftText: When good things increase, so do those who consume them; what then is the profit to the owner, except to behold them with his eyes?
units.rightText: When goods increase, they are increased that eat them; and what advantage is there to the owner thereof, save the beholding of them with his eyes?

units.leftText: The sleep of the worker is sweet, whether he eats little or much, but the abundance of the rich man permits him no sleep.
units.rightText: The sleep of a laboring man is sweet, whether he eat little or much; but the fulness of the rich will not suffer him to sleep.

units.leftText: There is a grievous evil I have seen under the sun: wealth hoarded to the harm of its owner,
units.rightText: There is a grievous evil which I have seen under the sun, namely, riches kept by the owner thereof to his hurt:

units.leftText: or wealth lost in a failed venture, so when that man has a son there is nothing to pass on.
units.rightText: and those riches perish by evil adventure; and if he hath begotten a son, there is nothing in his hand.

units.leftText: As a man came from his mother’s womb, so he will depart again, naked as he arrived. He takes nothing for his labor to carry in his hands.
units.rightText: As he came forth from his mother’s womb, naked shall he go again as he came, and shall take nothing for his labor, which he may carry away in his hand.

units.leftText: This too is a grievous affliction: Exactly as a man is born, so he will depart. What does he gain as he toils for the wind?
units.rightText: And this also is a grievous evil, that in all points as he came, so shall he go: and what profit hath he that he laboreth for the wind?

units.leftText: Moreover, all his days he eats in darkness, with much sorrow, sickness, and anger.
units.rightText: All his days also he eateth in darkness, and he is sore vexed, and hath sickness and wrath.

units.leftText: Here is what I have seen to be good and fitting: to eat and drink, and to find satisfaction in all the labor one does under the sun during the few days of life that God has given him — for this is his lot.
units.rightText: Behold, that which I have seen to be good and to be comely is for one to eat and to drink, and to enjoy good in all his labor, wherein he laboreth under the sun, all the days of his life which God hath given him: for this is his portion.

units.leftText: Furthermore, God has given riches and wealth to every man, and He has enabled him to enjoy them, to accept his lot, and to rejoice in his labor. This is a gift from God.
units.rightText: Every man also to whom God hath given riches and wealth, and hath given him power to eat thereof, and to take his portion, and to rejoice in his labor—this is the gift of God.

units.leftText: For a man seldom considers the days of his life, because God keeps him occupied with the joy of his heart.
units.rightText: For he shall not much remember the days of his life; because God answereth him in the joy of his heart.

units.leftText: There is another evil I have seen under the sun, and it weighs heavily upon mankind:
units.rightText: There is an evil which I have seen under the sun, and it is heavy upon men:

units.leftText: God gives a man riches, wealth, and honor, so that he lacks nothing his heart desires; but God does not allow him to enjoy them. Instead, a stranger will enjoy them. This is futile and a grievous affliction.
units.rightText: a man to whom God giveth riches, wealth, and honor, so that he lacketh nothing for his soul of all that he desireth, yet God giveth him not power to eat thereof, but an alien eateth it; this is vanity, and it is an evil disease.

units.leftText: A man may father a hundred children and live for many years; yet no matter how long he lives, if he is unsatisfied with his prosperity and does not even receive a proper burial, I say that a stillborn child is better off than he.
units.rightText: If a man beget a hundred children, and live many years, so that the days of his years are many, but his soul be not filled with good, and moreover he have no burial; I say, that an untimely birth is better than he:

units.leftText: For a stillborn child enters in futility and departs in darkness, and his name is shrouded in obscurity.
units.rightText: for it cometh in vanity, and departeth in darkness, and the name thereof is covered with darkness;

units.leftText: The child, though neither seeing the sun nor knowing anything, has more rest than that man,
units.rightText: moreover it hath not seen the sun nor known it; this hath rest rather than the other:

units.leftText: even if he lives a thousand years twice over but fails to enjoy his prosperity. Do not all go to the same place?
units.rightText: yea, though he live a thousand years twice told, and yet enjoy no good, do not all go to one place?

units.leftText: All a man’s labor is for his mouth, yet his appetite is never satisfied.
units.rightText: All the labor of man is for his mouth, and yet the appetite is not filled.

units.leftText: What advantage, then, has the wise man over the fool? What gain comes to the poor man who knows how to conduct himself before others?
units.rightText: For what advantage hath the wise more than the fool? or what hath the poor man, that knoweth how to walk before the living?

units.leftText: Better what the eye can see than the wandering of desire. This too is futile and a pursuit of the wind.
units.rightText: Better is the sight of the eyes than the wandering of the desire: this also is vanity and a striving after wind.

units.leftText: Whatever exists was named long ago, and it is known what man is; but he cannot contend with one stronger than he.
units.rightText: Whatsoever hath been, the name thereof was given long ago; and it is known what man is; neither can he contend with him that is mightier than he.

units.leftText: For the more words, the more futility — and how does that profit anyone?
units.rightText: Seeing there are many things that increase vanity, what is man the better?

units.leftText: For who knows what is good for a man during the few days in which he passes through his fleeting life like a shadow? Who can tell a man what will come after him under the sun?
units.rightText: For who knoweth what is good for man in his life, all the days of his vain life which he spendeth as a shadow? for who can tell a man what shall be after him under the sun?

units.leftText: A good name is better than fine perfume, and one’s day of death is better than his day of birth.
units.rightText: A good name is better than precious oil; and the day of death, than the day of one’s birth.

units.leftText: It is better to enter a house of mourning than a house of feasting, since death is the end of every man, and the living should take this to heart.
units.rightText: It is better to go to the house of mourning than to go to the house of feasting: for that is the end of all men; and the living will lay it to his heart.

units.leftText: Sorrow is better than laughter, for a sad countenance is good for the heart.
units.rightText: Sorrow is better than laughter; for by the sadness of the countenance the heart is made glad.

units.leftText: The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, but the heart of fools is in the house of pleasure.
units.rightText: The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning; but the heart of fools is in the house of mirth.

units.leftText: It is better to heed a wise man’s rebuke than to listen to the song of fools.
units.rightText: It is better to hear the rebuke of the wise, than for a man to hear the song of fools.

units.leftText: For like the crackling of thorns under the pot, so is the laughter of the fool. This too is futile.
units.rightText: For as the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of the fool: this also is vanity.

units.leftText: Surely extortion turns a wise man into a fool, and a bribe corrupts the heart.
units.rightText: Surely extortion maketh the wise man foolish; and a bribe destroyeth the understanding.

units.leftText: The end of a matter is better than the beginning, and a patient spirit is better than a proud one.
units.rightText: Better is the end of a thing than the beginning thereof; and the patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit.

units.leftText: Do not be quickly provoked in your spirit, for anger settles in the lap of a fool.
units.rightText: Be not hasty in thy spirit to be angry; for anger resteth in the bosom of fools.
leftNotes: 7:9 Hebrew in the bosom of fools

units.leftText: Do not say, “Why were the old days better than these?” For it is unwise of you to ask about this.
units.rightText: Say not thou, What is the cause that the former days were better than these? for thou dost not inquire wisely concerning this.

units.leftText: Wisdom, like an inheritance, is good, and it benefits those who see the sun.
units.rightText: Wisdom is as good as an inheritance; yea, more excellent is it for them that see the sun.

units.leftText: For wisdom, like money, is a shelter, and the advantage of knowledge is that wisdom preserves the life of its owner.
units.rightText: For wisdom is a defence, even as money is a defence; but the excellency of knowledge is, that wisdom preserveth the life of him that hath it.

units.leftText: Consider the work of God: Who can straighten what He has bent?
units.rightText: Consider the work of God: for who can make that straight, which he hath made crooked?

units.leftText: In the day of prosperity, be joyful, but in the day of adversity, consider this: God has made one of these along with the other, so that a man cannot discover anything that will come after him. The Limits of Human Wisdom
units.rightText: In the day of prosperity be joyful, and in the day of adversity consider; yea, God hath made the one side by side with the other, to the end that man should not find out anything that shall be after him.

units.leftText: In my futile life I have seen both of these: A righteous man perishing in his righteousness, and a wicked man living long in his wickedness.
units.rightText: All this have I seen in my days of vanity: there is a righteous man that perisheth in his righteousness, and there is a wicked man that prolongeth his life in his evil-doing.

units.leftText: Do not be overly righteous, and do not make yourself too wise. Why should you destroy yourself?
units.rightText: Be not righteous overmuch; neither make thyself overwise: why shouldest thou destroy thyself?

units.leftText: Do not be excessively wicked, and do not be a fool. Why should you die before your time?
units.rightText: Be not overmuch wicked, neither be thou foolish: why shouldest thou die before thy time?

units.leftText: It is good to grasp the one and not let the other slip from your hand. For he who fears God will follow both warnings.
units.rightText: It is good that thou shouldest take hold of this; yea, also from that withdraw not thy hand: for he that feareth God shall come forth from them all.

units.leftText: Wisdom makes the wise man stronger than ten rulers in a city.
units.rightText: Wisdom is a strength to the wise man more than ten rulers that are in a city.

units.leftText: Surely there is no righteous man on earth who does good and never sins.
units.rightText: Surely there is not a righteous man upon earth, that doeth good, and sinneth not.

units.leftText: Do not pay attention to every word that is spoken, or you may hear your servant cursing you.
units.rightText: Also take not heed unto all words that are spoken, lest thou hear thy servant curse thee;

units.leftText: For you know in your heart that many times you yourself have cursed others.
units.rightText: for oftentimes also thine own heart knoweth that thou thyself likewise hast cursed others.

units.leftText: All this I tested by wisdom, saying, “I resolve to be wise.” But it was beyond me.
units.rightText: All this have I proved in wisdom: I said, I will be wise; but it was far from me.

units.leftText: What exists is out of reach and very deep. Who can fathom it?
units.rightText: That which is, is far off and exceeding deep; who can find it out?

units.leftText: I directed my mind to understand, to explore, to search out wisdom and explanations, and to understand the stupidity of wickedness and the folly of madness.
units.rightText: I turned about, and my heart was set to know and to search out, and to seek wisdom and the reason of things, and to know that wickedness is folly, and that foolishness is madness.

units.leftText: And I find more bitter than death the woman who is a snare, whose heart is a net, and whose hands are chains. The man who pleases God escapes her, but the sinner is ensnared.
units.rightText: And I find more bitter than death the woman whose heart is snares and nets, and whose hands are bands: whoso pleaseth God shall escape from her; but the sinner shall be taken by her.

units.leftText: “Behold,” says the Teacher, “I have discovered this by adding one thing to another to find an explanation.
units.rightText: Behold, this have I found, saith the Preacher, laying one thing to another, to find out the account;

units.leftText: While my soul was still searching but not finding, among a thousand I have found one upright man, but among all these I have not found one such woman.
units.rightText: which my soul still seeketh, but I have not found: one man among a thousand have I found; but a woman among all those have I not found.

units.leftText: Only this have I found: I have discovered that God made mankind upright, but they have sought out many schemes.”
units.rightText: Behold, this only have I found: that God made man upright; but they have sought out many inventions.

units.leftText: Who is like the wise man? Who knows the interpretation of a matter? A man’s wisdom brightens his face, and the sternness of his face is changed.
units.rightText: Who is as the wise man? and who knoweth the interpretation of a thing? A man’s wisdom maketh his face to shine, and the hardness of his face is changed.

units.leftText: Keep the king’s command, I say, because of your oath before God.
units.rightText: I counsel thee, Keep the king’s command, and that in regard of the oath of God.

units.leftText: Do not hasten to leave his presence, and do not persist in a bad cause, for he will do whatever he pleases.
units.rightText: Be not hasty to go out of his presence; persist not in an evil thing: for he doeth whatsoever pleaseth him.

units.leftText: For the king’s word is supreme, and who can say to him, “What are you doing?”
units.rightText: For the king’s word hath power; and who may say unto him, What doest thou?

units.leftText: Whoever keeps his command will come to no harm, and a wise heart knows the right time and procedure.
units.rightText: Whoso keepeth the commandment shall know no evil thing; and a wise man’s heart discerneth time and judgment:

units.leftText: For there is a right time and procedure to every purpose, though a man’s misery weighs heavily upon him.
units.rightText: for to every purpose there is a time and judgment; because the misery of man is great upon him:

units.leftText: Since no one knows what will happen, who can tell him what is to come?
units.rightText: for he knoweth not that which shall be; for who can tell him how it shall be?

units.leftText: As no man has power over the wind to contain it, so no one has authority over his day of death. As no one can be discharged in wartime, so wickedness will not release those who practice it.
units.rightText: There is no man that hath power over the spirit to retain the spirit; neither hath he power over the day of death; and there is no discharge in war: neither shall wickedness deliver him that is given to it.

units.leftText: All this I have seen, applying my mind to every deed that is done under the sun; there is a time when one man lords it over another to his own detriment. Fear God (Isaiah 8:11–15|ISA 8:11-15*)
units.rightText: All this have I seen, and applied my heart unto every work that is done under the sun: there is a time wherein one man hath power over another to his hurt.

units.leftText: Then too, I saw the burial of the wicked who used to go in and out of the holy place, and they were praised in the city where they had done so. This too is futile.
units.rightText: So I saw the wicked buried, and they came to the grave; and they that had done right went away from the holy place, and were forgotten in the city: this also is vanity.
leftNotes: 8:10 Some Hebrew manuscripts, LXX, and Vulgate; most Hebrew manuscripts were soon forgotten

units.leftText: When the sentence for a crime is not speedily executed, the hearts of men become fully set on doing evil.
units.rightText: Because sentence against an evil work is not executed speedily, therefore the heart of the sons of men is fully set in them to do evil.

units.leftText: Although a sinner does evil a hundred times and still lives long, yet I also know that it will go well with those who fear God, who are reverent in His presence.
units.rightText: Though a sinner do evil a hundred times, and prolong his days, yet surely I know that it shall be well with them that fear God, that fear before him:

units.leftText: Yet because the wicked do not fear God, it will not go well with them, and their days will not lengthen like a shadow. God’s Ways Are Mysterious
units.rightText: but it shall not be well with the wicked, neither shall he prolong his days, which are as a shadow; because he feareth not before God.

units.leftText: There is a futility that is done on the earth: There are righteous men who get what the actions of the wicked deserve, and there are wicked men who get what the actions of the righteous deserve. I say that this too is futile.
units.rightText: There is a vanity which is done upon the earth, that there are righteous men unto whom it happeneth according to the work of the wicked; again, there are wicked men to whom it happeneth according to the work of the righteous: I said that this also is vanity.

units.leftText: So I commended the enjoyment of life, because there is nothing better for a man under the sun than to eat and drink and be merry. For this joy will accompany him in his labor during the days of his life that God gives him under the sun.
units.rightText: Then I commended mirth, because a man hath no better thing under the sun, than to eat, and to drink, and to be joyful: for that shall abide with him in his labor all the days of his life which God hath given him under the sun.

units.leftText: When I applied my mind to know wisdom and to observe the task that one performs on the earth — though his eyes do not see sleep in the day or even in the night —
units.rightText: When I applied my heart to know wisdom, and to see the business that is done upon the earth (for also there is that neither day nor night seeth sleep with his eyes),

units.leftText: I saw every work of God, and that a man is unable to comprehend the work that is done under the sun. Despite his efforts to search it out, he cannot find its meaning; even if the wise man claims to know, he is unable to comprehend.
units.rightText: then I beheld all the work of God, that man cannot find out the work that is done under the sun: because however much a man labor to seek it out, yet he shall not find it; yea moreover, though a wise man think to know it, yet shall he not be able to find it.

units.leftText: So I took all this to heart and concluded that the righteous and the wise, as well as their deeds, are in God’s hands. Man does not know what lies ahead, whether love or hate.
units.rightText: For all this I laid to my heart, even to explore all this: that the righteous, and the wise, and their works, are in the hand of God; whether it be love or hatred, man knoweth it not; all is before them.

units.leftText: It is the same for all: There is a common fate for the righteous and the wicked, for the good and the bad, for the clean and the unclean, for the one who sacrifices and the one who does not. As it is for the good, so it is for the sinner; as it is for the one who makes a vow, so it is for the one who refuses to take a vow.
units.rightText: All things come alike to all: there is one event to the righteous and to the wicked; to the good and to the clean and to the unclean; to him that sacrificeth and to him that sacrificeth not; as is the good, so is the sinner; and he that sweareth, as he that feareth an oath.
leftNotes: 9:2 LXX, Syriac, and Vulgate; Hebrew does not include and the bad.

units.leftText: This is an evil in everything that is done under the sun: There is one fate for everyone. Furthermore, the hearts of men are full of evil and madness while they are alive, and afterward they join the dead.
units.rightText: This is an evil in all that is done under the sun, that there is one event unto all: yea also, the heart of the sons of men is full of evil, and madness is in their heart while they live, and after that they go to the dead.

units.leftText: There is hope, however, for anyone who is among the living; for even a live dog is better than a dead lion.
units.rightText: For to him that is joined with all the living there is hope; for a living dog is better than a dead lion.

units.leftText: For the living know that they will die, but the dead know nothing. They have no further reward, because the memory of them is forgotten.
units.rightText: For the living know that they shall die: but the dead know not anything, neither have they any more a reward; for the memory of them is forgotten.

units.leftText: Their love, their hate, and their envy have already vanished, and they will never again have a share in all that is done under the sun. Enjoy Your Portion in This Life
units.rightText: As well their love, as their hatred and their envy, is perished long ago; neither have they any more a portion for ever in anything that is done under the sun.

units.leftText: Go, eat your bread with joy, and drink your wine with a cheerful heart, for God has already approved your works:
units.rightText: Go thy way, eat thy bread with joy, and drink thy wine with a merry heart; for God hath already accepted thy works.

units.leftText: Let your garments always be white, and never spare the oil for your head.
units.rightText: Let thy garments be always white; and let not thy head lack oil.

units.leftText: Enjoy life with your beloved wife all the days of the fleeting life that God has given you under the sun — all your fleeting days. For this is your portion in life and in your labor under the sun.
units.rightText: Live joyfully with the wife whom thou lovest all the days of thy life of vanity, which he hath given thee under the sun, all thy days of vanity: for that is thy portion in life, and in thy labor wherein thou laborest under the sun.
leftNotes: 9:9 Or futile; twice in this verse

units.leftText: Whatever you find to do with your hands, do it with all your might, for in Sheol, where you are going, there is no work or planning or knowledge or wisdom.
units.rightText: Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might; for there is no work, nor device, nor knowledge, nor wisdom, in Sheol, whither thou goest.

units.leftText: I saw something else under the sun: The race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong; neither is the bread to the wise, nor the wealth to the intelligent, nor the favor to the skillful. For time and chance happen to all.
units.rightText: I returned, and saw under the sun, that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, neither yet bread to the wise, nor yet riches to men of understanding, nor yet favor to men of skill; but time and chance happeneth to them all.

units.leftText: For surely no man knows his time: Like fish caught in a cruel net or birds trapped in a snare, so men are ensnared in an evil time that suddenly falls upon them. Wisdom Is Better than Strength
units.rightText: For man also knoweth not his time: as the fishes that are taken in an evil net, and as the birds that are caught in the snare, even so are the sons of men snared in an evil time, when it falleth suddenly upon them.

units.leftText: I have also seen this wisdom under the sun, and it was great to me:
units.rightText: I have also seen wisdom under the sun on this wise, and it seemed great unto me:

units.leftText: There was a small city with few men. A mighty king came against it, surrounded it, and built large siege ramps against it.
units.rightText: There was a little city, and few men within it; and there came a great king against it, and besieged it, and built great bulwarks against it.

units.leftText: Now a poor wise man was found in the city, and he saved the city by his wisdom. Yet no one remembered that poor man.
units.rightText: Now there was found in it a poor wise man, and he by his wisdom delivered the city; yet no man remembered that same poor man.

units.leftText: And I said, “Wisdom is better than strength, but the wisdom of the poor man is despised, and his words are not heeded.”
units.rightText: Then said I, Wisdom is better than strength: nevertheless the poor man’s wisdom is despised, and his words are not heard.

units.leftText: The calm words of the wise are heeded over the shouts of a ruler among fools.
units.rightText: The words of the wise heard in quiet are better than the cry of him that ruleth among fools.

units.leftText: Wisdom is better than weapons of war, but one sinner destroys much good.
units.rightText: Wisdom is better than weapons of war; but one sinner destroyeth much good.

units.leftText: As dead flies bring a stench to the perfumer’s oil, so a little folly outweighs wisdom and honor.
units.rightText: Dead flies cause the oil of the perfumer to send forth an evil odor; so doth a little folly outweigh wisdom and honor.

units.leftText: A wise man’s heart inclines to the right, but the heart of a fool to the left.
units.rightText: A wise man’s heart is at his right hand; but a fool’s heart at his left.

units.leftText: Even as the fool walks along the road, his sense is lacking, and he shows everyone that he is a fool.
units.rightText: Yea also, when the fool walketh by the way, his understanding faileth him, and he saith to every one that he is a fool.

units.leftText: If the ruler’s temper flares against you, do not abandon your post, for calmness lays great offenses to rest.
units.rightText: If the spirit of the ruler rise up against thee, leave not thy place; for gentleness allayeth great offences.

units.leftText: There is an evil I have seen under the sun — an error that proceeds from the ruler:
units.rightText: There is an evil which I have seen under the sun, as it were an error which proceedeth from the ruler:

units.leftText: Folly is appointed to great heights, but the rich sit in lowly positions.
units.rightText: folly is set in great dignity, and the rich sit in a low place.

units.leftText: I have seen slaves on horseback, while princes go on foot like slaves.
units.rightText: I have seen servants upon horses, and princes walking like servants upon the earth.

units.leftText: He who digs a pit may fall into it, and he who breaches a wall may be bitten by a snake.
units.rightText: He that diggeth a pit shall fall into it; and whoso breaketh through a wall, a serpent shall bite him.

units.leftText: The one who quarries stones may be injured by them, and he who splits logs endangers himself.
units.rightText: Whoso heweth out stones shall be hurt therewith; and he that cleaveth wood is endangered thereby.

units.leftText: If the axe is dull and the blade unsharpened, more strength must be exerted, but skill produces success.
units.rightText: If the iron be blunt, and one do not whet the edge, then must he put to more strength: but wisdom is profitable to direct.

units.leftText: If the snake bites before it is charmed, there is no profit for the charmer.
units.rightText: If the serpent bite before it is charmed, then is there no advantage in the charmer.

units.leftText: The words of a wise man’s mouth are gracious, but the lips of a fool consume him.
units.rightText: The words of a wise man’s mouth are gracious; but the lips of a fool will swallow up himself.

units.leftText: The beginning of his talk is folly, and the end of his speech is evil madness.
units.rightText: The beginning of the words of his mouth is foolishness; and the end of his talk is mischievous madness.

units.leftText: Yet the fool multiplies words. No one knows what is coming, and who can tell him what will come after him?
units.rightText: A fool also multiplieth words: yet man knoweth not what shall be; and that which shall be after him, who can tell him?

units.leftText: The toil of a fool wearies him, for he does not know the way to the city.
units.rightText: The labor of fools wearieth every one of them; for he knoweth not how to go to the city.

units.leftText: Woe to you, O land whose king is a youth, and whose princes feast in the morning.
units.rightText: Woe to thee, O land, when thy king is a child, and thy princes eat in the morning!

units.leftText: Blessed are you, O land whose king is a son of nobles, and whose princes feast at the proper time— for strength and not for drunkenness.
units.rightText: Happy art thou, O land, when thy king is the son of nobles, and thy princes eat in due season, for strength, and not for drunkenness!

units.leftText: Through laziness the roof caves in, and in the hands of the idle, the house leaks.
units.rightText: By slothfulness the roof sinketh in; and through idleness of the hands the house leaketh.

units.leftText: A feast is prepared for laughter, and wine makes life merry, but money is the answer for everything.
units.rightText: A feast is made for laughter, and wine maketh glad the life; and money answereth all things.

units.leftText: Do not curse the king even in your thoughts, or curse the rich even in your bedroom, for a bird of the air may carry your words, and a winged creature may report your speech.
units.rightText: Revile not the king, no, not in thy thought; and revile not the rich in thy bedchamber: for a bird of the heavens shall carry the voice, and that which hath wings shall tell the matter.

units.leftText: Cast your bread upon the waters, for after many days you will find it again.
units.rightText: Cast thy bread upon the waters; for thou shalt find it after many days.

units.leftText: Divide your portion among seven, or even eight, for you do not know what disaster may befall the land.
units.rightText: Give a portion to seven, yea, even unto eight; for thou knowest not what evil shall be upon the earth.

units.leftText: If the clouds are full, they will pour out rain upon the earth; whether a tree falls to the south or to the north, in the place where it falls, there it will lie.
units.rightText: If the clouds be full of rain, they empty themselves upon the earth; and if a tree fall toward the south, or toward the north, in the place where the tree falleth, there shall it be.

units.leftText: He who watches the wind will fail to sow, and he who observes the clouds will fail to reap.
units.rightText: He that observeth the wind shall not sow; and he that regardeth the clouds shall not reap.

units.leftText: As you do not know the path of the wind, or how the bones are formed in a mother’s womb, so you cannot understand the work of God, the Maker of all things.
units.rightText: As thou knowest not what is the way of the wind, nor how the bones do grow in the womb of her that is with child; even so thou knowest not the work of God who doeth all.
leftNotes: 11:5 Or As you do not know the way the spirit comes to the bones

units.leftText: Sow your seed in the morning, and do not rest your hands in the evening, for you do not know which will succeed, whether this or that, or if both will equally prosper. Enjoy Your Years
units.rightText: In the morning sow thy seed, and in the evening withhold not thy hand; for thou knowest not which shall prosper, whether this or that, or whether they both shall be alike good.

units.leftText: Light is sweet, and it pleases the eyes to see the sun.
units.rightText: Truly the light is sweet, and a pleasant thing it is for the eyes to behold the sun.

units.leftText: So if a man lives many years, let him rejoice in them all. But let him remember the days of darkness, for they will be many. Everything to come is futile.
units.rightText: Yea, if a man live many years, let him rejoice in them all; but let him remember the days of darkness, for they shall be many. All that cometh is vanity.

units.leftText: Rejoice, O young man, while you are young, and let your heart be glad in the days of your youth. Walk in the ways of your heart and in the sight of your eyes, but know that for all these things God will bring you to judgment.
units.rightText: Rejoice, O young man, in thy youth, and let thy heart cheer thee in the days of thy youth, and walk in the ways of thy heart, and in the sight of thine eyes; but know thou, that for all these things God will bring thee into judgment.

units.leftText: So banish sorrow from your heart, and cast off pain from your body, for youth and vigor are fleeting.
units.rightText: Therefore remove sorrow from thy heart, and put away evil from thy flesh; for youth and the dawn of life are vanity.

units.leftText: Remember your Creator in the days of your youth, before the days of adversity come and the years approach of which you will say, “I find no pleasure in them,”
units.rightText: Remember also thy Creator in the days of thy youth, before the evil days come, and the years draw nigh, when thou shalt say, I have no pleasure in them;

units.leftText: before the light of the sun, moon, and stars is darkened, and the clouds return after the rain,
units.rightText: before the sun, and the light, and the moon, and the stars, are darkened, and the clouds return after the rain;

units.leftText: on the day the keepers of the house tremble and the strong men stoop, when those grinding cease because they are few and those watching through windows see dimly,
units.rightText: in the day when the keepers of the house shall tremble, and the strong men shall bow themselves, and the grinders cease because they are few, and those that look out of the windows shall be darkened,

units.leftText: when the doors to the street are shut and the sound of the mill fades away, when one rises at the sound of a bird and all the daughters of song grow faint,
units.rightText: and the doors shall be shut in the street; when the sound of the grinding is low, and one shall rise up at the voice of a bird, and all the daughters of music shall be brought low;

units.leftText: when men fear the heights and dangers of the road, when the almond tree blossoms, the grasshopper loses its spring, and the caper berry shrivels — for then man goes to his eternal home and mourners walk the streets.
units.rightText: yea, they shall be afraid of that which is high, and terrors shall be in the way; and the almond-tree shall blossom, and the grasshopper shall be a burden, and desire shall fail; because man goeth to his everlasting home, and the mourners go about the streets:

units.leftText: Remember Him before the silver cord is snapped and the golden bowl is crushed, before the pitcher is shattered at the spring and the wheel is broken at the well,
units.rightText: before the silver cord is loosed, or the golden bowl is broken, or the pitcher is broken at the fountain, or the wheel broken at the cistern,

units.leftText: before the dust returns to the ground from which it came and the spirit returns to God who gave it.
units.rightText: and the dust returneth to the earth as it was, and the spirit returneth unto God who gave it.

units.leftText: “Futility of futilities,” says the Teacher. “Everything is futile!” The Whole Duty of Man
units.rightText: Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher; all is vanity.

units.leftText: Not only was the Teacher wise, but he also taught the people knowledge; he pondered, searched out, and arranged many proverbs.
units.rightText: And further, because the Preacher was wise, he still taught the people knowledge; yea, he pondered, and sought out, and set in order many proverbs.

units.leftText: The Teacher searched to find delightful sayings and to record accurate words of truth.
units.rightText: The Preacher sought to find out acceptable words, and that which was written uprightly, even words of truth.
leftNotes: 12:10 Or and sought to write what was upright and true

units.leftText: The words of the wise are like goads, and the anthologies of the masters are like firmly embedded nails driven by a single Shepherd.
units.rightText: The words of the wise are as goads; and as nails well fastened are the words of the masters of assemblies, which are given from one shepherd.

units.leftText: And by these, my son, be further warned: There is no end to the making of many books, and much study wearies the body.
units.rightText: And furthermore, my son, be admonished: of making many books there is no end; and much study is a weariness of the flesh.

units.leftText: When all has been heard, the conclusion of the matter is this: Fear God and keep His commandments, because this is the whole duty of man.
units.rightText: This is the end of the matter; all hath been heard: Fear God, and keep his commandments; for this is the whole duty of man.

units.leftText: For God will bring every deed into judgment, along with every hidden thing, whether good or evil.
units.rightText: For God will bring every work into judgment, with every hidden thing, whether it be good, or whether it be evil.
